bib.title: Harness-IF: Evaluating Instruction Following Across Instruction Surfaces in Coding Agents

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: Extraction worked. 26 pages, 89,074 chars. I read pp. 1-11 (main text), the reference list was skimmed for origins, and appendices (A-G) were read selectively. I grepped the appendices for denominators, judge settings, E0, clusters, non-coding results and test-retest, and did not read them line by line. Nothing was garbled. No embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "Harness-IF: Evaluating Instruction Following Across Instruction Surfaces in Coding Agents". First author Zining Huang (ByteDance Seed and Tsinghua). Co-authors from ByteDance Seed and Peking University; corresponding author Shen Yan. Stated date July 15, 2026; arXiv 2608.11727v1, 12 Aug 2026. No venue, so preprint. The release location is "given in a later version".

CORE CLAIM: Aggregate instruction-following scores overstate compliance, because an agent may follow a rule it was going to follow anyway. Scoring only against-prior rules (AP-Acc) lowers every model's score by a model-specific margin. The paper also reports that instruction placement does not follow prompt depth.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Main panel: 12 models, 60 multi-turn coding items, 3 rounds = 2,160 runs, 40,104 verdict rows (37,616 eligible pass/fail; 19,449 against-prior). Metric is per-rule pass rate. Acc ranges 72.1% (StepFun-3.5) to 85.9% (Claude-Opus-4.7). AP-Acc ranges 66.1% (Seed-2.0-Pro) to 78.6% (Opus-4.7). The gap is positive for all 12, from +3.6 (GLM-5.1) to +7.4 (Seed-2.0-Pro), mean 5.81. Opus-4.7 is 85.9 vs 78.6; GPT-5.5 is 83.1 vs 77.0.
2. Grading: deterministic checks cover 13.3% of verdicts. A GPT-5.2 judge uses a three-vote majority, so 86.8% of rows involve the judge. Prior control leaves the top build unchanged but swaps three adjacent rank pairs (2-3, 4-5, 11-12). On common support (2,430 of 3,342 keys, 72.7%), item-clustered 95% intervals for the gap stay positive per model. Adjacent-model comparisons are all unresolved.
3. Reliability limits: test-retest ICC is 0.725 across models and 0.599 across agent-item cells. Agreement under a judge swap is 62.1% (kappa 0.163, 116 paired verdicts). An earlier human audit gave 69.0% agreement (kappa 0.515, 919 rows). Claude-GPT agreement is kappa 0.4717 on n=65. Appendix: the mean per-cell Acc range across rounds is 15.6pp.
4. E0 surface-precedence pilot: 9 older model builds, 4 synthetic conflict pairs, 916 runs (458 per direction, 889 decisive), deterministic scoring only. SP, PF and UI tie at mean rank 2.22 (20/9), TD is 3.78 and SD is 4.56. The full ordering holds in 9,652 of 10,000 bootstrap resamples, but only 6 of 9 individual builds reproduce it.
5. Failures: shortfall rules (require, minimum) carry 77.1% of the 8,440 failures. Overstep rules carry 20.8%. Fail rates are similar (23.8% vs 20.8%), so the skew is exposure. Output control is the hardest family (70.9% vs 82.6% for quantitative). Commanding rules score 76.0% vs 90.6% for preferences.

QUOTES
- p.1 abstract: "every model is worse on against-prior rules, by 3.6 to 7.4 points (mean 5.81)".
- p.9: "That the user instruction only ties for first is inconsistent with such an account." (a prompt-depth account).

LIMITS (authors and mine)
- The harness is not the variable in the main panel. Surfaces are assigned by admissibility, not randomised, so the panel supports only descriptive surface stratification. The controlled relocation (E0) is small, synthetic and run on older builds.
- Items were chosen from 80 candidates for difficulty and discriminativeness, which the authors call selection optimism.
- The prior labels come from a 9-build zero-injection probe, or from curation. That probe cohort overlaps the evaluated panel (5 of 9 share an identifier) and the E0 builds. The authors call the labels behavioral strata, not training provenance.
- Absolute levels are instrument-specific because of the judge dependence. The claims rest on cross-model patterns, not on rankings.
- Not shown: a model-vs-harness comparison, or the same model under different agent harnesses. The 12 models run in one harness setup. The paper names no harness product in the main text; Appendix D covers the serving configuration. The non-coding panel (40 cases, 1,428 trajectories, case-macro 65.8-84.8%) is not pooled with the coding results.

BUILDS ON: IFEval (Zhou 2023), FollowBench, InfoBench, ComplexBench, IFBench, AgentIF, and the instruction hierarchy (Wallace 2024). It also builds on IHEval (Zhang 2025), SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, and BFCL/AppWorld/tau-bench.

BEST-FIT SECTION OF 06-evaluating-agents.md: the paragraph around line 245 ("The harness is a component too, so report model and harness together"). Alternatively, the "Grade the outcome by state, not by words" section at line 106. The note already has harness effects from Terminal-Bench, AutoLab (line 316) and ARTEMIS. It lacks two things:
- Rule-level scoring with a prior (default-behaviour) control, which asks whether the agent would have done this anyway.
- Placement of instructions across surfaces (system prompt, project file, tool and skill descriptions), with E0 showing that tool and skill descriptions lose conflicts. This is the "where the rule lives" axis, distinct from model-vs-harness.
- A caveat on judge dependence (kappa 0.163 under a judge swap) is also not in the note.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 6 (p.10), E0 mean conflict ranks (SP, PF and UI tied at 2.22, TD 3.78, SD 4.56). Figure 7 (appendix) shows the per-agent Acc vs AP-Acc gap, but it is secondary.
